title: Maekawa
statement: At a flat vertex, mountains and valleys differ by exactly two.
why: Going round the vertex the paper turns 360°. Each valley adds +180°, each mountain −180°, so they must net to ±360°.
example: Four creases meet; three are valleys and one is a mountain.
details: Count only creases that are folded (M or V), not reference lines.
It follows that the number of creases at a flat vertex is even.

exceptions.title: Wet-folding and curves
exceptions.text: Curved creases bend the paper instead of folding it flat.

title: Kawasaki
statement: Alternate angles around a flat vertex sum to 180°.
why: Walking round the vertex, each fold reflects the paper; after a full turn you must be back where you started.
details: Measure the sectors between consecutive creases around the vertex.
Combined with Maekawa this is the local test for flat-foldability.

exceptions.title: Curved creases
exceptions.text: Curved-crease models are not straight-line flat folds.

exceptions.title: 3D shaping
exceptions.text: Non-flat final shapes do not need Kawasaki at every vertex.

title: Even degree
statement: Every interior vertex of a flat fold has an even number of creases.
why: Each crease flips the paper over; an odd number of flips cannot close up.
example: A vertex with three creases can never fold flat.
details: Boundary vertices on the paper edge are exempt.

title: Big-little-big
statement: Creases on both sides of a strictly smallest angle have opposite types.
why: If both were valleys, the two big neighbouring sectors would collide when the small one folds.
example: A 45° sector between a 90° and a 90° sector needs one mountain and one valley.
details: Applies to each sector that is smaller than both its neighbours.

exceptions.title: 3D shaping
exceptions.text: Models that end non-flat can break it.

title: Two-colourable
statement: A flat-foldable pattern's faces can be coloured with two colours.
why: After folding, each face is either face-up or face-down; folds always switch between the two.
example: The square base alternates colours around the centre.
details: Equivalent to every interior vertex having even degree.

exceptions.title: Kirigami
exceptions.text: Cuts can separate faces so the colouring no longer has to close up.

title: No self-intersection
statement: Layers can never pass through each other.
why: Paper is solid. A valid fold needs a stacking order of all layers that never crosses.
example: Two flaps folded into the same pocket must nest, not cut through.
details: Finding a valid layer order for a whole pattern is NP-hard (Bern and Hayes, 1996).
CreaseLens checks only local rules; the 3D preview may show layers crossing.

exceptions.title: Tessellations
exceptions.text: Twists can be flat-foldable but not rigid-foldable; panels must bend while folding.

title: Huzita–Justin axioms
statement: Seven ways to define a single fold from points and lines.
why: They describe every line you can find with one fold, so diagrams can be followed exactly.
example: Axiom 2: fold so one point lands on another.
details: 1. Fold through two points.
2. Fold one point onto another.
3. Fold one line onto another.
4. Fold through a point, perpendicular to a line.
5. Fold through a point, placing another point onto a line.
6. Place two points onto two lines at once (solves cubics).
7. Place a point onto a line, perpendicular to another line.

exceptions.title: Rectangles
exceptions.text: Planes and dollar-bill folds start from rectangles but use the same axioms.

title: Diagram symbols
statement: Yoshizawa–Randlett symbols say which fold to make.
why: One shared notation lets anyone read diagrams in any language.
example: A dashed line is a valley; a dash-dot line is a mountain.
details: Valley fold: dashed line, arrow with a solid head.
Mountain fold: dash-dot line, arrow with a hollow half-head.
Fold and unfold: arrow that returns.
Turn over: looping arrow.
Reverse, squash, petal and sink folds each have their own arrows.

exceptions.title: Action models
exceptions.text: Moving parts are shown with motion arrows that are not folds.

title: Paper rules
statement: One square sheet, no cuts, no glue.
why: Pure origami makes everything from folding alone.
example: The crane uses one uncut square.
details: Many traditions relax these rules on purpose.

exceptions.title: Rectangles
exceptions.text: Planes and money folds start from rectangles.

exceptions.title: Wet-folding
exceptions.text: Damp thick paper is shaped into curves.

exceptions.title: Action models
exceptions.text: Models such as the flapping bird are designed to move.
